utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow the proceedings fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good morning to the -- my learned friends of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I represent Mr. Naser Oric. We are accompanied by our legal assistant, Ms. Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have one preliminary, and that's to update the Trial Chamber on the Rule 94 bis motion for the Prosecution filed and that Defence had submitted a response. The Prosecution and the Defence have had the time to have discussions, and our understanding is at this point, the Defence has agreed to withdraw their motion -- their reply to our motion, and that they will submit a different reply which is basically to accept the expert statement of Dr. Stankovic and the attached autopsy report. And then the Prosecution has agreed, if they do file that response, then we will refrain from calling Dr. Stankovic to come to the Tribunal to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose -- thank you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I imagine we'd need the leave of the Chamber in one form or another to withdraw that response and file a new one. We would still obviously want to take, as I mentioned to my learned friend, take a couple of points, or at least have the right to raise a couple of points in relation to the report that's set out in the current response, and we'll reiterate them in this response. But it's just merely to reserve our position with respect to the piece of paper allegedly found on the corpse and identification by a family member. We want to preserve our position on those two points. But apart from that, the arrangement is precisely as Ms. Sellers has outlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you have our authority to replace your response with the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll file that very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have one preliminary as well, and it's to anticipate slightly because it concerns the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it may even be prudent to go into private session for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jankovic. Welcome back. We are going to continue with your testimony today, and I ask Mr. Jones, who is co-counsel defending Naser Oric, to commence with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just have a few general questions about the project, as it was described yesterday, which you undertook, and then we'll look at some of your photographs. Now, firstly, just to pin down precisely when you took the photographs, you told us yesterday that they were taken in July and August of 1994, but in your statement to ICTY investigators, you said the entire project went on until July 1996. So my question is: Were all the photographs taken in 1994 or were some, perhaps, taken as late as 1996?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case that we are dealing with now, all photographs were taken in late August of 1994. The material was processed, and everything was completed in September, in view of the fact that we needed to put it down, we needed to type up the report, glue down the photographs. And all of that work was completed in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. Now, to summarise your work, and nothing that is said is intended as a criticism of you or your methods, but isn't it right you took 642 photographs of the alleged crime sites in July and August of 1994 and you're not able to say for a single one, are you, when any of the houses were damaged? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. They could have been damaged in 1994, 1993, 1992, or even before the war, for all we know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to pinpoint any of the years that you have mentioned. I simply am unable to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as well as not being able to say when any damage was caused, you're also not able to say, are you, who caused any damage. It could be men, women, adults, children, Muslims, Serbs, anyone.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, I wouldn't be able to say that, and I've mentioned so several times yesterday during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's clear, and that's why I would ask you why, in your report by yourself and Mr. Zvonko Dzurdumovic - which perhaps you could look at, it's P487 - in that report it was suggested that the damage to the property was destroyed due to "the very intensive combat activities of the Muslim military and paramilitary formations in 1992 and 1993," whereas, in fact, you don't know that, do you, and you can't say that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement, which can be found in line 4 of that report, I believe, was a result of the information that we had received from municipal authorities upon arriving in that area. This statement was not a result of our own analysis. This is just something that we heard from municipal authorities, from local guides. This is what they told us. Perhaps we should have been more specific about the source of that information in our report. But just so that you know, this is how it came to be included.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. So in summary, that's not something you're reporting, that's not a finding which you're reporting.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you didn't, in fact, sign the report, did you? I don't know if you recall, or if you want to look at it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that I did sign it, but you might have a copy which doesn't bear my signature. However, I did sign it. The report was written by Zvonko Dzurdumovic, and I think that my signature was the second one on the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. The copy I had doesn't have your signature, and I was wondering if that was why you hadn't signed it, because of this additional information. Right. Now, on the same subject, in the table which we saw, and also the map, that's headed "Table of Documented Burned and Destroyed Facilities During the Combat Activities in 1992 and 1993." So do you agree that, for the same reason, that's not a finding you made, that's not something you're reporting as being true, it's simply a title which appears?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly right. And it wouldn't have been logical to include that kind of a statement in the report. This is something that we heard from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Heard but didn't verify.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we heard, and it was almost impossible to verify it, at least in our line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, would you agree that there are many different ways in which property can be damaged during wartime, particularly if the houses are on the front lines, as these were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly agree with your statement. There are many ways in which these houses could have been damaged, and therefore, in our report, we did not specify the causes of damage. I don't think that that's specified in any part of our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. And if I set out a brief list, and you tell me if you agree that these might be causes of property damage generally: Damage caused by close combat activity from bullets, grenades, missiles, Zoljas. Would you agree, firstly, with that list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such causes were certainly possible. Yesterday, we looked at one of the photographs and I tried to tell you this precisely. It's difficult to base a conclusion on one of the photographs, but I saw all of the buildings at the time. And my conclusion was that they had been damaged in different ways. I did not make this conclusion in relation to every specific building or a description of the building as we found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So you concluded that the buildings had been damaged in different ways, so there wasn't any pattern, there wasn't any system, to how the houses had been destroyed, as far as you could see.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if my very generalised opinion is of any assistance to this Court. I think there were about three different ways the damage came about. I can't talk about the respective percentages, but there were several different ways that led us to have certain beliefs and opinions on how damage had come about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for the matter of clarification, are you now referring only to houses which have been shown yesterday, only on photos which have been shown here, or are you referring to your whole -- to all photos which you made? I think there were about 500, something like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last thing I said before you addressed me, Your Honour, what I had in mind was the entirety of photographs that we took and the entirety of buildings that we visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in the area you photographed, I think you told us that most of the occupants of the houses had abandoned their houses either during or shortly after the attack, and then didn't return for some time. So would that be correct, firstly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I said yesterday that, when we photographed these houses and when we marked them on our maps, we did not find the actual owners. I'm not talking about the period between 1992 and 1994, but rather about the specific point in time when we were doing our work. That was the point in time I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was wondering whether you had learned that many of these houses had been abandoned for a long period of time, at the time you came to photograph them, and that therefore the weather had taken its effect. Without a roof, the rain, wind, and snow had caused a lot of damage.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the weather was definitely an important factor. If you look at these photographs, you will see that there are different seasons, factors such as frost and humidity caused important changes to these buildings, making them exceedingly difficult to discuss. Now, as for the exact extent of changes visible in a certain photograph, it's very difficult for me to express myself in terms of percentages. But I do know there were significant differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. That's helpful. Now, I think you also acknowledged that when these houses were abandoned, there were signs that people had come by and strip the people of building materials, for example, the window frame, the roof tiles, maybe the door, any timber. Is that a phenomenon that you're familiar with or that you observed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, which I found very interesting, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you also see, as you travelled through this area, that there was a lot of building work, and actually observe people taking materials from deserted or abandoned houses and building themselves new roofs and now extensions and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether I actually saw someone taking construction material away from a given site. The answer is I didn't. But we did find buildings in certain places that were substantially ruined, and it was clear enough that someone had, in the meantime, covered the building from the outside, the owner perhaps, in order to protect it from the elements and such changes, as we referred to in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In some of the photographs, there's even the suggestion that a house has been rebuilt or a roof has been replaced as a result of it having been destroyed before. But isn't it right that, as far as anything which you know, you don't know whether a roof was replaced because the owner wanted a new roof, or whether a house was rebuilt because the owner wanted to rebuild his house. That's not something you can help us with, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I can, in fact, help you with that. Why was it that I concluded that the owner had merely tried to protect his house, to preserve it from further decay? Why? Because no further work was done on the house, and there were no changes or extensions. The essential features of the building remained the same. So the way I interpreted this was, the owner took urgent steps to try to preserve the condition of the house as it was, and perhaps give themselves a chance, at a later date, to carry out further repairs. That was my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: If you saw someone who had a newly tiled roof, you wouldn't be able to say, would you, whether that person had had a not very satisfactory roof or an old roof and they'd seen an abandoned house with very nice roof tiles and they'd gone along and helped themselves and given themselves a new roof? That's not something which you would know, unless you were provided some specific information. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, I am not really in a position to tell you where a given house owner obtained the construction material for his own house. But I am in a position to tell you that the building was damaged in precisely that way on account of the blackenings and dark spots or blots that we saw above certain windows and door frames. And that's why I'm telling you they merely used sheeting to protect their house from the elements, to preserve it from further decay. You could see that in some places, the roof had burned through, or maybe the roof had, in fact, been torn down. I really don't know, but I'm sure that the reason I'm giving you is the reason why the house was covered in sheeting, or whatever material was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Well, what I'm getting at is this: Didn't you sometimes base yourself, when you say in the captions to your photographs that a house has been rebuilt after some destruction has occurred, you were basing yourself partly on what people told you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The captions reflect our own impressions. If you've had a thorough look, if you've gone carefully through our documents, you must have realised that there are certain discrepancies between the captions. They're not the same for each building. Some buildings were substantially damaged and could no longer be used or inhabited. My caption in that case was "House Destroyed." If it was a matter of partial destruction, and the house could quickly be rebuilt, my caption was "Partially Destroyed." What I wish to say is that, at the time I tried to distinguish between the different degrees of destruction at first sight, on first impression, just like that. And this is something that I tried to specify. I believed at the time that this was an adequate approach for a case like this, and given the nature of the documents that we were expected to draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. You also mentioned yesterday that there was possibly a compensation aspect, ultimately, to this project; that if someone's house was documented as being destroyed during combat activities, then they be entitled to compensation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would you agree that in many cases, there would be a financial motive for people to misinform you about how damage occurred to property, or that a particular property belonged to a particular person?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object on the basis that this is speculative at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you are right, Ms. Richardson. I would either rephrase the question or leave it, omit it, completely, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll move on and come back to it in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You also told us that you thought, for this project to be viable, if you like, that what should have been done is both documenting what people said about how damage occurred to the property as well as having fire experts and other experts attending to provide a proper examination. I think you even said that the exercise would be pointless without that component. So my question is: Given those -- that those things were not done which, in your opinion, should have been done, do you consider that this project was, at best, incomplete and, at worst, a failure?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, of course, have my own opinion on this. We are looking at a very large number of houses spread throughout an area. It really depends on what you want to achieve with these files; it really depends on what an individual owner can attain in terms of his rights or entitlements, such as compensation. This would have been a good start, to take a photograph of their damaged houses. I do believe that I said at the outset of my testimony yesterday that we had given a recommendation to the municipal authorities that they should set up their own commissions that would visit all the sites, all the buildings, and try to establish the cause of damage, make lists of damage, be it furniture, construction material, cattle, anything of value that used to be there. And then use these two, including the initial document, to make a complete file, to see the whole thing through, establish the cause of damage and thus continue this process that we had only begun. That was the way we reasoned at the time about this project.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, I'm going to move around a bit, so I'm sure you can follow me. I have a couple of questions just about your training as well. You explained yesterday your task, how you would normally be directed to take pictures by an investigating judge, so I think we're clear about that. But just to be clear, you have no training as a fire expert, do you, in analysing causes of fire, seats of fire, whether they're caused by human agency or by some other cause? You wouldn't hold yourself out as a fire expert.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, in our school in Belgrade, there is a subject that is taught which relates to all the different areas covered by the work of a crime technician. Once you've passed that exam, you have a set of basic skills that allow you to draw conclusions on certain phenomena, but they do not give you any degree of expertise in terms of carrying out any further work in the lab or perhaps drawing up an expert opinion on a given case. This is definitely not something I was trained for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. If I understand correctly, your training was really to enable you to do your job as a technician, as a photographer, as a scene-of-crimes officer, to do your job properly, so you know roughly -- so that you'd know what to be looking for. Would that be a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Even if we look at the case at hand, we never even broached the subject of how the fire came about to begin with. We looked at the very first thing. We tried to capture the image of the place as it was by taking a photograph representing a general, broad view of the location itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, thank you. It was really because you were asked yesterday, and you confirmed, that you had participated in investigations of 200 fires, and so my question was, really, your participation was limited to taking photographs and that sort of thing, wasn't it? You weren't investigating the seat of the fire in those cases.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That goes without saying. In our work, we confined ourselves to what a crime technician should do, and that -- I'm saying that in relation to all the fires that we spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us how you used local residents to identify who were the occupants of houses, and we have that table with the names of the people who identified the houses in each hamlet or village. In many cases, you only had one person to identify all the houses, didn't you, in a hamlet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically, but I think there were about ten guides for the entire area. I can't remember the specific number of guides for each individual building, but I think there were a total of about ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we have one example as Najdan Mladzenovic identified 16 houses in Hranca. I'm going to ask you a bit about Hranca in a moment. But did you check the information that the person gave you about ownership against any official register of home ownership? In other words, did you verify the occupancy information that you received?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't verify that. However, in view of the fact that we were advised by the municipal authorities as to who our guides would be for specific areas, naturally, we assumed that those people really knew the area well, and that our documentation could be used in the following way: You could use other methods to verify and see for yourself; you were now in a position to actually call one of the owners and verify this information with the owners themselves. After 1994, back in Belgrade, by coincidence, I had further contacts with people from the area. They had, of course, no idea that anything like this had been done at all. I asked them where they were from, they said from such and such a hamlet. I showed them the photographs, and they would then say, Oh, yes, this is my father's house. Now, it was results like these that led me to believe that we had actually done our job quite well, and that we had not gone wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, if I understand what you've said correctly, you had a somewhat random confirmation from time to time of certain photographs that were correctly labeled in terms of ownership, but you're not saying, are you, that you verified the 642 houses by some secondary source, that your primary source was correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that I'm not saying that. It's not that I'm not saying that. The fact is we didn't verify ownership after we finished our work. The reason was that the documents were to be forwarded to the persons that they had been drafted for, after all. And then this person would be able - that's what we hoped - to do the checks and verify everything himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I asked -- we'll take the example of Hranca. Are you aware that Hranca is a Muslim village from which Muslims were expelled in May of 1992, and that their houses were burnt. Is that, firstly, something you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you asked me today about the individual places we visited, I find it very difficult to tell you about the respective percentages or about the mixed population of certain villages. This was just not something that I was familiar with. I was in the area for the first time in my life. That's one thing. Secondly, I didn't look into that at all. I did say in my testimony yesterday, and I'll repeat it for you, we knew that there were certain areas where the different ethnicities lived together. And it was precisely for this reason that I was adamant that there should be an international presence in our project. It was my desire at the time - it still is and will always be - that such projects should be carried out by a variety of different institutions which would enable them to cover an area thoroughly and to avoid such discrepancies as we see today in relation to this project. That would make our work a lot easier, and yours too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. The reason I ask is, let's take the example of Hranca, and your table says that Najdan Mladzenovic was your guide. My point is really this: That if there were burnt Muslim houses, and Najdan Mladzenovic said, That's the house of Mr. Simic, that's the house of Mr. Jovanovic and told you they were Serb houses, you simply wouldn't know, would you? And it wasn't something you verified.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying now is possible, that goes without saying. However, I will give you my general view on this whole thing. The work we carried out in the field, as I said yesterday, our work in the field, international organisations refused to take part, but they did monitor our work. Whenever we went to an area, and I suppose if you called the guides and asked them the questions, that they will have to answer, then we certainly took into account the fact that certain houses that were not owned by a person that you may now claim is the owner, the international organisations refused to take part in our work but maybe there will be another task, another job, where they will have a chance to get involved and make a greater contribution to the life of other communities. If you superimpose these two jobs, then you end up covering the entire area thoroughly. That was always my opinion. I stated this opinion clearly at our meetings with the local authorities and back in Belgrade. I realised that the UN were familiar with the lay of the land. I copied some of their maps and reports, and I realised that those were the same areas. I'm in a position to guarantee that this is, indeed, an opinion that I stated in no uncertain terms at all of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right, well, I'm sure that's correct, and I take your word for it. I may have to ask you to keep your answers a bit shorter, though, because we'd like to finish in the next half hour, or so. So, if possible, if you could keep your answers a bit shorter.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I still want to ask you a bit about your project in relation to destruction to Muslim villages and houses. Now, travelling through this area, Bratunac, Kravica, et cetera, you no doubt travelled through Glogova and other Muslim villages where houses had been damaged, where mosques had been destroyed, that sort of thing. It's right, isn't it, that you didn't take photographs of destroyed and burned Muslim houses in Glogova or elsewhere or of destroyed mosques.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember specifically about Glogova, but we did not photograph such buildings. If we had, they would now be part of our file. Each photograph that we took, each negative that was made, was later developed and now forms part of the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this is -- right. So if you -- when you were looking around this area with your local guide and you saw a destroyed house and your local guide said that was a Muslim house that was burned or a mosque that was dynamited, would you just put your camera down and walk away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be a bit harsh, especially considering what I explained to you a moment ago. I would not have laid down my camera, I would not have tried to avoid it. If you want us to be brief about this, I believe I've already explained my position on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let me come at it this way, and it is important. The committee which tasked you with taking photographs was called the Committee for the Information on the Committed Crimes against Humanity and International Law, and you were tasked -- I'm taking that from your report, and you were tasked with getting information on the damage caused during the combat activities in the region. So the committee is not a committee dealing only with crimes against Serbs, is it? And your mandate didn't say, only look at crimes against Serb property. So my question is: Did you -- and it's not a criticism -- but did you and Mr. Dzurdumovic decide to include your mandate to exclude property of Muslims, or did the committee make it clear to you that you were not to photograph damaged Muslim property?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly not a decision that's Zvonko Dzurdumovic and I made, that is, not to photograph the other houses. When we were given this task, they told us that the task was about Serb houses. I have to go back to my previous answer, and I'm restating my case now, and will continue to do so in the future. My general position on this is that other agencies should be involved on these projects so we don't have to go over the whole thing five times. And this would also allow us to have a better general impression of the situation. Now, that is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And, firstly, there's no need to restate your position, and it's understood. The reason I'm asking is that, in your work in Belgrade, you are, are you not, a crime technician, pure and simple, and politics play no part in your work? But wasn't this assignment different in that it wasn't neutral fact-finding and photographing, but it was a war zone which Serbs had been involved, and your project was a government initiative, initiated by the Republika Srpska, and so there was an initiative, there was a public relations exercise behind this project, namely, to show that Serbs were also victims in this war. That's my question to you. Were you aware of an ideological background to your work?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may. Mr. Jones has finally put the question to the witness. It seems like he's -- he seems to be making a number of statements prior to, and I think it seems to compound the question being put to the witness. I think finally we got to the question, but I would ask that he be instructed to keep his answers short. It seems that the questions are very compound, and there are a number of statements in them. And if we are to be fair to the witness, I think we should ask him one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know if instructing me to keep my questions short would be terribly fair to my liberty as a professional. If my question is too long, I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll go straight to the witness. Do you consider yourself, do you feel confused by the way Mr. Jones is putting his questions to you, particularly the last couple of questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not confused at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the impression I had as well, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm just saying for the record when the witness answers yes or no, or provides an explanation, then it's a bit confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay, but I think more or less we are following, and when the witness says yes or no in unequivocal fashion or manner, we will intervene. But I don't think there have been such cases so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can rephrase my question shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But don't take it in any way as kind of interference on the part of the Tribunal, but I don't think I would censor you in the way that you have been putting your questions, particularly the last few questions. To be honest with you, those were the areas I intended to cover myself had you not dealt with them in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I tried to take several points at once, but I can put a short question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you feel, Mr. Jankovic, that there was a sort of pressure on you in conducting this exercise, a sort of public relations pressure from the government?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood what this was all about, what you were discussing. I will tell you what my position is, and also the position of my colleague, with whom I worked. At that time, while this was happening, and also today, I personally was never interested in political aspects of that work. So anything that you might want to ask me about that are not relevant, from my point of view. In my personal position, and also in my work, I take the view that there's no room for politics in that. Our work has absolutely no political aspect whatsoever. This is something that doesn't even come into our minds. I hope you understand that. Even in the country where I live, and in the city where I live, that still holds true. However, if it's important for the Court, I can tell you that I do not belong to any political party. I'm simply a professional, and this has been my attitude my entire life.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that candid answer. It's really this which I'm -- one of the things I'm driving at, which is this: That you took 642 photographs, and it would appear from that that there was a very large number of houses which were damaged. We're going to look at some of the photographs in a moment, but I would suggest to you that, actually, a large number of those houses aren't particularly damaged. And so my question, really, was whether there was a pressure on you to produce a very elevated number of photographs on the part of the committee which had commissioned you, if you follow.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me for saying so, but you could have found an answer to your question in my description of how we worked. No pressure was ever exerted upon us. When we went out in the field to work with the guide, the guide would tell us, This is a house that belongs to such and such person. And throughout that time, our work was a product of cooperation between three people working in the field. There was no pressure whatsoever coming from any side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Okay, well, two short subjects before we look at some of the photographs. First of all, you told us yesterday that you didn't photograph all damaged houses. You accepted that maybe other houses were damaged which you did not photograph. But it's also true, isn't it, that there were many undamaged houses which you didn't photograph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were houses that were not damaged and there were also houses whose owners were not known to the guide. As simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you also told us yesterday that, when you were speaking of fire damage to a house, that you weren't basing yourself just on the photograph but also on your memory, since you were there. It's right, isn't it, that you were -- when you were taking these photographs, you were rushing from house to house, from dawn 'til dusk, working 16 hours a day. Firstly, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. From dawn, as soon as it became light, then we would take photographs, make sketches. I would write down my notes, based on which we produced the documentation that you see today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This was ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And these are 600 or so houses which, is it right, you had never seen before and which were in an area which was unfamiliar to you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I probably would be able to find these houses if I used a map. But if you were to ask me, for example, where the house of such and such owner is located, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So isn't it right that you don't actually have any reliable recollection today of each of these houses, where they were, what you saw at the time, beyond what you can simply see in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll look at some of the photographs now, and again it will only be a sampling. You were shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I can ask the booth to switch on to Defence mode so that we can show -- we'll deal with the photographs electronically, and hopefully zap through them quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were shown at least two photographs yesterday in which you agreed that a projectile had probably hit the building. That was one of them. And I'll just read -- for the record, I'll just read the last four digits of the ERN. They are all 0108. So this is 7870, and also 7874, you were shown. And I think you agreed also there that the roof appeared to have been hit by a projectile. Now, you were also shown 01087838, if we could have a look at that. Now, there, when you were asked about that, you referred to blackening above the window, suggesting smoke. But you didn't say anything about what appears to be a hole in the roof. Do you see what appears to have been a patched-up hole? And would you agree that that could have been a shell hitting the house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let us remain in the domain of what was possible. Yes, indeed, this is possible, what you said. But when I mentioned the black marks above the door and the window, you will be able to see for yourself that, on the upper floor, there are no such black marks. And I'm not going to draw a conclusion for you, I will leave that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I won't ask you to express opinions about causes of damage or anything like that, for all the reasons we discussed yesterday. It will just be a question of you confirming appearances. Now, if we look at 01087950, we'll look at a few others and just tell us whether you agree that they could also show shell damage. Do you agree with that picture, 7950?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, but we would need to see what the house looks like from the other side. I believe that it was impossible to take the picture from the other side, and this is why it was photographed only from this side. Let us remain in the realm of what is possible, and this is the only kind of an answer I can provide. If that is of any assistance to you, we can proceed with an analysis of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. It will be a question of just briefly looking at a number of photographs. 01087796. Again, isn't the substantial damage to the upper storey compatible with a shell or some heavy calibre artillery hitting the top of the house?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we stated yesterday. Once again, we are still assuming or supposing that that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, there are a number of photographs of this nature, and I won't go through all of them. It was just to be illustrative. Now, your report also claims to document a desecration of monuments. If we could just look briefly at 01087835. This is a photograph of a plaque, the top part of which is intact and the bottom of which is destroyed. Now, surely, you'd agree that any vandal wielding a hammer could smash a plaque - Serb, Muslim, Croat, Gypsy, anyone? You're not testifying, or appearing to suggest, that that plaque was damaged during combat activities, are you, in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we look at 01087927, and there are a number of photographs of this nature, you have photographs which are meant to show desecration of religious monuments. But the fact is, isn't it, that that photo is equally consistent with a stray bullet, shot in combat, hitting the gravestone, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I also put to you earlier that a lot of the photographs you took which bear captions that houses were destroyed are only, if anything, partially damaged houses. We can have a quick sampling. 01088042. We see some bullet holes there, and perhaps some window frames that have been taken. But that's not a destroyed house, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a house, we couldn't call it that. As for the extent of damage, I would leave it for somebody else to comment upon it. But this is not a house that is inhabitable, not anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's look at 01088085. That house is, surely, habitable, isn't it? It's even got window frames. Just a small bit of damage to the plaster.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, there's a caption under the photograph precisely what we concluded. These are school apartments that had been damaged and then repaired. If you were to ask me whether I remember this house, I would have answered no; however, that's precisely why I took notes. This house was repaired partially, which means that its previous condition was somewhat different. What it was like, I don't know, and I didn't write down anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how do you know that it's been repaired?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states here, "Repaired." That means that some work had been done. If it were up to me to conclude what was done, then I would say that a new roof was put in place and that some further work was being done. I assume that new windows were installed. As you can see, it has a gutter which was not tied in with the rest of the construction. The roof was set in place; however, the gutter was not linked to the rest of the roof construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was, how do you know that this house, and many of the other houses which are described as being repaired, how do you know that they've been repaired? Surely, you're not basing yourself just on your own caption.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on my personal observations and also on what we heard when we were there. If somebody tells you that a new beam was put in place a month ago, then, yes, you draw certain conclusions based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's what I was getting at earlier when I was asking whether you based yourself on what people told you, because a person -- if a person did tell you something like that, you basically just had to take their word for it, didn't you? You had no way of verifying.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain cases, we were unable to draw a conclusion. We had to rely on their words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why, also, I was asking earlier about compensation, because isn't it right that someone who says, Yes, my house was destroyed, I repaired it, their photograph appears in your album, that they now have a claim for compensation based on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object again, speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we can look at 01088088, same point again, really. To all appearances, that's a perfectly good house. In fact, it's a school, as I see from the caption. You say it's been renovated, but you can't tell us anything about what state it was in before it was renovated, can you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully understand your question. Rest assured, I do understand it. However, I can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Given that we're short of time, I'm going to skip through and just really see a few more pictures. If we could go to 01087912, and this goes to what you were told by your local guides about places. This is a photo of the primary school in Kravica. Now, did your guides tell you that that was the command of the 3rd Kravica Battalion, which was based in the school on the 7th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that we did not discuss these topics. You asked me about political aspects, and now I am adding a military aspect as well, because we might come to it eventually. These are issues that the commission did not deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we look at 01087898, I'll ask you in relation to that picture, 7898, whether you keep a -- whether you keep a record -- we'll have the picture in a second. Whether you keep a record of when each individual photograph was taken? Do you have a record of each photograph, of precisely when it was taken? That's the question, first of all, before we see the picture.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me to refer to my notes, I will be able to tell you the exact date when we visited this, and also the same for other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have your notes with you? Because for this photograph, this is the Kravica Oka warehouse, you may be aware, between 1.500 and 2.000 Muslims were killed in cold blood in July 1995, and so we would certainly be interested in verifying whether that picture was taken before or after. You told us your pictures were taken in 1994, but if you can verify for that picture that it was, indeed, taken then, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These photographs were definitely made in 1994. What I don't know is whether that was done on the 7th or on the 8th, because we began our work on the 7th of July and concluded on the 16th of July. I think that Kravica and Jezestica were done in the first stage of our work. If you allow me to refer to my notes, I will be able to tell you the exact date when this photograph was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you're sure of 1994, we can probably leave it there, given the shortness of time. If we could see 01088221.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have something I wish to add. You asked me whether I was sure that this was made in 1994. All of the photographs before you were made in 1994, in a very specific time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, thank you. It was just to check, because, as I asked you at the beginning, the project was completed in 1996, so that was why I wanted to be sure. Now, this photograph, I'm not even sure what we're supposed to be seeing there. My question is: How did you even know that there were any destroyed houses there when you took that picture?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was based on trust. We had to rely on what guides told us. That's the first thing. The second thing is that, from this distance, you were able to see that the house did not have the roof. If we were to enlarge this photograph, and we didn't visit these houses for the reasons stated yesterday and in my report, then let's leave it at that. Everybody can make their own conclusions about the report that we produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It was just really just to say this: Isn't it the case that sometimes it's not actually photographic evidence which you're presenting; in this case, its a photograph which is a proxy for documentary or testimonial evidence, namely, that photograph is representing that people told you there were destroyed houses there. The photograph doesn't actually show that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are very few such photographs in the file. If you were to go through the entire documentation, you would see that there may be just a couple of photographs like this. As far as I was concerned, I would have loved to go and see the houses themselves. However, as we had local guides, and they told us that it wasn't a good idea to go see those houses, then I hope you would agree with me that it was wise to follow their advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Thank you, Mr. Jankovic. As I say, nothing was a criticism of your professionalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. I'll try and make an effort to finish with the witness now. Is there re-examination, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, briefly. I don't know if you want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Then we'll have a break, a 25-minute break, and then I suppose you will be here for not more than 15 minutes, Mr. Jankovic, and then you can go back home. Twenty-five minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, we are late, but we were in camera discussing, of course, the matter that was raised earlier in relation to the next witness' testimony. Yes, re-examination, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. Jankovic, regarding your training as a crime scene technician, and in this case where you documented a number of damaged houses pursuant to the request of the commission, I'd just like to clarify with respect to your training, and that includes on-the-job training as well as courses and exams you've taken. Now, is it a fact that those courses also included training in -- basic training in fires and how fires are started, et cetera, so that this type of training and instructions will assist you in better performing your job as a crime scene technician? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So the training doesn't arrive -- rise to the level of that of an expert, but it is pretty significant, since it assists with your job. And when you arrive at a particular crime scene, the photographs that you take very often become evidence in a number of cases.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about damage to the houses, and we -- there were pictures shown to you by myself yesterday, as well as Mr. Jones today, regarding the damage. Some of the photographs were indicative of weaponry being used and which caused the damage. But it was also put to you today about weather damage. And could you tell us if it was your impression, as you took those photographs, that the major cause of the damage to the home was, indeed, from the weather or other natural elements?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already commented on that today. The passage of time, as well as the climatic conditions, were factors which contributed to the fact that many indicia that might lead us to conclusions on how damage had come about changed. There was a lot of moisture, humidity, which affected the condition of the buildings because they were uncovered or unprotected. Then winter came along and there was frost. There was damage to the facades, to the walls. And this is something that I said in my testimony. I said clearly that any elements which might have initially been there for us to conclude how damage had come about were, in fact, annulled or wiped up by the weather.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. But this was not the case with respect to all of the houses. In fact, I believe you testified that there was some indication that there had been a fire or that the damage had occurred as a result of weaponry. So the additional damages that you're referring to, just for clarification, the further damage which resulted from the weather, was just in addition to the initial damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, this is comment by my learned friend. Secondly, unless we have a specific photograph to know what we're talking about, I don't know how this witness can answer in the abstract for 642 houses. There are specific photographs which we were thinking of showing the witness where it appears that houses have just decayed with the passage of time. I think this exercise can only be meaningfully carried out if we're talking about specific houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Jones' point, and perhaps a photograph would be appropriate at this time. But I would just like the witness to comment on, just generally, whether it was his observation that, while some of the homes appear, to him, damaged from the weather, in fact, that there was other damage, and that other damage was either from fire or weaponry, the very reason that he was taking the photograph to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a perfectly legitimate question. Go ahead. Witness, please answer the question, and then we'll go to specifics, because you've got to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- you're being generic, as it is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we photographed the buildings, that represented their average condition. If we were to comment on each and every one of the buildings, we would then have to use all the photographs, which is too extensive a task. If I were to use specific photographs at this point in time, as in right now, it would be very difficult for me to say how certain changes came about, whether it's because of the poor quality of construction material that was used for building a certain house or other causes. I think that would definitely take us too far, and I think all such considerations would be pointless for the case in hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. At the time you took the photograph, while you were being escorted by the guide -- and that guide, I take it, was a local person who was aware of the owner of the house and had some information about how the damage occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would remain within the sphere of hearsay. The guide tells us that a certain house was set on fire. You accept that, but proving that is a different thing, because what information is based on is just the guide's knowledge of a certain event. But we would have to investigate the whole case in order to reach the truth of how damage occurred in the first place, which means that you would have to enlist the help of a number of different experts and teams.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. We understand that. With respect to the photographs that you, in fact, did take, there was, with the very naked eye, that is, evidence that a fire had occurred. I believe you testified about this yesterday. And as well as the fact that damage could have occurred from weaponry --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I finish the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Which photograph are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones. Finish the question, but witness, don't answer it before I tell you so. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just if I could have a moment, Your Honour. I'll just repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to the photographs that you did take, was it clear to you at the time, based on the limited knowledge you have with respect to fires, which I suppose may be more than the average person because you've taken courses and you have some training, were you able to see for yourself that a fire had occurred in some of the photographs that you had taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you still have an objection, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see how possibly we can go through this exercise unless we know which photographs. I mean, perhaps the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- the witness is simply being asked out of 642 photographs, one or two seem to show some evidence that at some stage a fire may have occurred, then I suppose he can answer that. But the exercise seems completely futile if we're not talking about specific houses and specific photographs. How can he comment, Yes, I saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's really a lot of the testimony of this witness is marginal. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If my learned friend could refer to a specific photograph, then there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you, Mr. Jones, when you present it this way, because the question is perfectly legitimate insofar as the witness is being asked a very simple question. When you photographed a building, and you tell us that you photographed it because, to you, there was damage, and you told us here that there was signs that a fire -- that there had been a fire inside those particular buildings --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's certainly very far from the case that this witness has said he only took photographs of buildings which appeared to be damaged by fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, he didn't say that. He said that -- but he's being asked about those that he told us showed signs of a fire. And he's being asked now, I mean don't ask me why, but he's being asked now to tell us whether this is just mere speculation or whether it's the fruit of his limited expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that format, the question is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's perfectly legitimate. And then if we want to go into specifics, we can go into specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness could be permitted to answer the question at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to read it out to you again? Or are you also trained enough to remember the questions that were put to you and answer them five minutes after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand the question only too well, and I've been following your communication with the other parties. I'll tell you as follows: As any other layman, it should be very easy for me to tell if a house burned down or not, or if there was a fire inside the house. How this fire was started, or what caused it, now that's a tough nut to crack. It can be due to negligence, it can be due to weather conditions, or a variety of other factors. Right now we can't answer these questions in relation to many of these buildings, that is for sure. We are no longer in a position to say now what originally caused those fires, that's certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jankovic. And my question with respect to the fires is not what caused the fire but whether, in fact, there was a fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I will ask the usher's assistance at this time to just place this photograph on the ELMO. And it's ERN 01087846. This was a photograph that was shown yesterday to Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, as you're -- as you're looking at that photograph, it was suggested to you that there was reconstruction, and in fact you did testify that there was reconstruction to some of these houses. My question is: As you're looking at that particular photograph, could you tell us if, in addition to the roof that is -- which appears to you at the time and appears in this photograph to be new, could you also tell whether there is -- there was a fire in that building, without going into what could have caused it, because we know that you're not qualified to testify to what the cause was. But could you tell us from that photograph whether you can see evidence of a fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at this photograph, we can say, just by looking at the photograph, that the part of the house around one of the doors and the small window on the left-hand side, we can assume that there is a lavatory behind that toilet, if we look at these things, it should be possible for us to say that yes, indeed, there was a fire inside this house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So despite the fact that there is a new roof on this building, it does indicate that there was a fire. I guess that would be my question and my point.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. You testified as well yesterday that there are three types of houses that you photographed where there was damage, and it was suggested to you on cross-examination that some of these houses that you photographed were, in fact, not totally destroyed. My question to you is: You testified that you went into some of the houses. And could you tell us if the houses that you went into were habitable?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the houses that I went into were not habitable. Their interior was virtually destroyed. There was no paint on the walls, and everything that you normally find inside a house was no longer there. So that was the condition of those houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the type of material, building material, that is used to construct a house, and, for instance, if it is a brick house and a fire had taken place, based on your experience - and if you don't know the answer, please tell us that you don't know and you're not qualified - but would the entire house burn down or would part of the structure remain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we talk about the type of house that you have just referred to, there would be sections still standing; usually, walls and the central petitions. But the light roof structure, which is made of wooden beams, and other such light wooden structures were gone. As simple as that. That was at least what we observed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And if the house had been made of material other than brick or wood, such as the final group that you testified, made of mud or attached, what evidence would remain if a fire occurred in that house? In other words -- just as an addition, to assist you with answering, would any of the walls or the roof or anything else remain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said yesterday that there were three types of houses: Mud and straw; secondly, those partially built of brick and stone; and thirdly, modern houses built of reinforced concrete. The third type would usually bear visible marks which we then interpret in certain photographs. The old-type houses opposite the modern ones, very old, the modern straw houses would bear no such visible marks because they were, as a rule, completely ruined. Sometimes you had only sections of the wooden beams that remained, whereas some were completely destroyed and were reduced to nothing but rubble overgrown by weeds. Unless someone actually takes you there and tells you that there was a house there, there used to be a house, you wouldn't be likely to realise that yourself, without being told.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time I'd like the usher's assistance, if you can just present this to the witness on the ELMO. For the record, it's ERN 01088470.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The photograph at the very bottom, Mr. Jankovic, if you could turn your attention to that photograph. Now, based on your memory, is this the type of structure -- construction that you referred to as a straw construction? Or do you recall what type of material this house would have been made of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a mud and straw building, but there are sections remaining, what is practically the basement, because it's on a slope, the house is on a slope. And then when a house like this is built, you have stones of irregular shape that are laid down as a foundation. There is a certain number of mud and straw houses - I can't give you the exact number now - that were built on flat ground, and they don't have this base sticking out, which happens to remain here just because the house was built on a slope. This is, indeed, one such case, and I could tell you more about it, but I'm not sure how relevant it is at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. So my question is: Had a fire occurred to this particular type of structure, what you see remaining is what would remain. In other words, it wouldn't remain as the type of structure -- the type of walls that would remain in a brick house, but if a fire occurred to a building built of this type of material, this is what would remain, what we're looking at here, 470.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what would remain. If you tried to dig into this base that you can see in the photograph, you would find bits and pieces that belonged to the house, layers of the original house, in other words. I'm not going into any details now. I'm not sure how useful an exercise it would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm almost finished, Your Honour. Just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the reconstruction of buildings that you photographed, particularly the school, you were advised that the reason that the school was under reconstruction, were you not, was because there had been damage to the school.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this is the same information you received with respect to buildings where there was new construction or buildings that were visibly under repair.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the few places where we found a number of people. This is in the centre of the village, and that's why I remember it so well. This is not a random case. There were several people assembled there building things, and that was precisely why I said it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. If you could just direct your attention to the monitor, I'd like to show photographs, ERN 01087836 and 01087837. Now, do you recall taking photographs of what's seen before you, these monuments?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the particular moment I photographed these, but yes, I was the one who did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And these monuments -- and you took more than one such photograph; do you recall if that's correct? You took several.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember specifically now. We usually pay attention to detail, and in this particular case it was possible for us to do so. So we must have taken a general-view photograph. I believe I saw one of these in your files. And then we focused on the inscription. And then you have one close-up and then another even closer close-up. And the inscription contains names of people related in some way to this memorial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I take it that you took this photograph because this memorial had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we were told. It was damaged, but we were told that someone else had caused the damage. And that was the reason for us taking this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the photograph before you, does that depict damage caused by a stray bullet or -- if you recall at the time you took the photograph, do you -- do you recall what, perhaps, may have caused damage to this monument?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I considered how I could approach this question, then my conclusion would be that it was hit by a missile, like I commented in relation to some other photographs. But there would be some sort of a caption or a comment, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, I have one further question for you. With respect to the verification of the houses, the local person who took you to various houses, did the local person who escorted you attempt to identify houses, or did the person seem certain as to who the owners of the houses were? And I understand that there were various people who escorted you throughout the various villages. Did these local guides, in general, seem uncertain about who the houses -- the owners of the houses were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, I can't remember each and every one of the guides. There were cases, however, where the guide was uncertain about who the owner was, and whenever the guide was uncertain, I refused to take any photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Richardson. Judge Brydensholt has not got any questions. Judge Eser, I understand, has a few questions. Judge Eser, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, you made it quite clear to us that you do not consider yourself an expert in explaining the reasons of a fire, or whether there was a fire, or something else. Nevertheless, I took it that, apart from your professionalism as a photographer, that you collected quite a lot of ability, perhaps, to see more when seeing a building which is damaged, that you may be more able to recognise certain things that a normal man on the street would recognise, that you may have become -- got a clearer view to certain things. Am I correct in assuming this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, to the point that you complained on various occasions that, unfortunately, there was no international cooperation in your project, would you think that your work as a photographer was impaired by this lack of international cooperation? So the authenticity of your taking pictures, was it somehow impaired that there had not been any international people around you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As concerns the authenticity of my photographs, the authenticity itself did not require any cooperation from the international organisations. When I referred to international cooperation, I referred to the authenticity of the entire project. That would have been a logical sequence for me which would have shed a great deal of light in the future on everything that occurred in the area, this area, as well as some other areas with which I was involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the damages and the situation, the appearance of the houses, you have been asked whether these damages may not have been -- occurred in a certain period of time, or that these houses may have been abandoned a long period of time ago, which would suggest that perhaps the houses had been abandoned, let's say, ten years before that. Now, would you say that, at least to your own experience as a photographer, that even if you cannot say it was in the year 1992, 1993, or 1994, that these damages have at least occurred in this period and not, let's say, ten -- many, 10, 20 years earlier?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in order to establish something like that, it is not material that you be a photographer. You can base that on a great variety of elements. A great variety of different factors and elements might lead you to conclude whether the house -- whether a house was recently inhabited or had been abandoned long ago. If we speak about houses that don't even have a roof, or houses that appear to have sustained substantial damage, obviously, these cases are more difficult for you to draw conclusions on. It's easier to draw conclusions when you have more solidly built houses of which sections, at least, remained around the house itself, part of the door, windows, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My question was not completely answered yet. What I wanted to ask you: When it was suggested to you that some of the houses may have been abandoned, and I'm citing you, have been -- not you, I'm citing the Defence, that some of the houses may have been abandoned a long period of time ago, how did you understand this long period of time? Does it mean within the years 1991 and 1994? Or a long period of time, that means even 10, 15 years earlier?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I understood the question of the Defence well, and I knew why I said that. When you have a local guide who knows the area well -- let me give you an example. There was a lady who was a teacher. I think that was in Jezestica. She knew the local live residents, children who lived in certain houses. So if she told you that somebody lived in a house in 1990 or 1991 or before that, and that had lived there permanently, you can do nothing else but rely on her words. And that's exactly what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. Mr. Jankovic, that brings us to an end. You lasted here more than the 15 minutes that I had promised you before the break, but in any case, we are finished.
