I do thank you for -- not only for having come over to give evidence in this case, but also for the frank and professional manner in which you have approached the subject of your testimony and the way you have answered the questions that were put to you. Your testimony has been extremely helpful to this Tribunal, and I thank you for that. I thank you, of course, on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, and also on behalf of the Tribunal in general. You will now be escorted out of the courtroom by Madam Usher, and I can assure you that you will receive all of the assistance that you require to facilitate your return back home and to your work as well as soon as possible. Once more, I thank you, and I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and everyone else in the courtroom, for a proper attitude. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we discussed earlier -- no, no, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thought Your Honour was addressing me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We discussed earlier on the matter that was raised by Mr. Jones, which was responded to by Ms. Sellers. We did that in private session. It relates to the next witness -- to the next witness. We have discussed the matter in camera during the break, and we are in a position to hand down an oral decision here and now, which is a unanimous decision, by the way. But I think that we ought to do this in private session, because it is a consequence of the discussion that we had before which was in private session, particularly because of what it deals with. So let's go into private session, and the decision will be handed down before the witness is admitted, obviously. And then we'll take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before I proceed any further, I want to make sure that you're receiving interpretation in your own language of what I am saying in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I also want to make sure that you are comfortable with that headset, and that the sound level is not too high or too low.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank you for having come over to this Tribunal to give evidence, which you are going to start giving very shortly. Before you sit down and you start giving -- you start with your testimony, our Rules require that you enter, that you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath to the effect that, in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration is being handed to you now by Madam Usher. Could I please ask you to read that text aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. You may sit down. Please take a seat. So you have been summoned to give evidence in this case against Naser Oric by the Office of the Prosecutor, but now you are a witness of this Tribunal. And your responsibility is only towards this Tribunal. Your responsibility is to tell us the truth, as you go along in the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The procedure is as follows: You will first be asked a set of questions by Ms. Sellers, who is one of the Prosecution -- members of the Prosecution team in this case, whom you have met already. She will then be followed by Madam Vidovic, who is the lead counsel for Naser Oric in this case. Your responsibility is -- your obligation is to answer all questions as fully and as truthfully as you can, to the best of your ability, and in so doing, you must distinguish between questions coming from the Prosecution and questions coming from the Defence. In other words, you do not have the freedom or the liberty to discriminate between one and the other. They are all doing their duty here, and your responsibility is to answer all questions truthfully, irrespective of who is putting them. If, at any time, you need a break, or if, at any time, there are questions that you would like not to answer, please look at us, the three Judges up here, and we will consider your request. I will tell you who we are. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from Malta, the island of Malta. To my right is Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt who comes from Denmark. To my left, I have Judge Albin Eser who comes from Germany. We welcome you here. And I now give the floor to Ms. Sellers, who can start with her direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would have two housekeeping things I'd like to present first. One is, could I ask the usher to please either lower the screen or remove the ELMO. I cannot see the witness' face. And the other is for purposes not of an exhibit that this witness will draw upon, but these are maps that will basically take care of the region which the testimony will concern. I'd like to hand those up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I guess it's appropriate now to say good afternoon to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means I took five minutes or six minutes on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would please ask the witness to state her full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Andja Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you also state your married name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Married last name is Obradovic, maiden name is Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to take the liberty of leading a bit of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Ms. Sellers, as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, I'd like to take you to April of 1992. Is it correct that at that time period you were living in Novo Selo, which is in the municipality of Zvornik, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And at that time period, did you live in a village where there were approximately 12 Muslim houses -- I'm sorry, 12 Bosnian Serb houses and about 150 Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you work at an embroidery company prior to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you cease to work at that embroidery company because the passageway was blocked and you were unable to get to work due to mounting military activity near Novo Selo, in Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Also, as a result of the budding military activity, did you live with your brother-in-law and your sister-in-law in the lower part of your village?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, for the sake of the Trial Chamber, would you please explain whether you received papers for working conscription from the Republika Srpska in the beginning of April 1992 -- I'm sorry, June 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Trial Chamber what types of official documents you did receive from the Republika Srpska government.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was there for the weekend to help in distributing the food to local residents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: When you said "distributing food to local residents," are you talking about residents who were military residents, are you talking about civilian residents, are you talking about refugees?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were you a part of an army battalion?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not, although they mentioned the 2nd Battalion. But I was not in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you wearing a uniform, or did you have a gun issued to you, as you were feeding these members or these civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That -- one moment, one moment, that may be a little bit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That may be particularly leading, Ms. Sellers, in that for at least three years I've had an opportunity to follow interpretation as we go along, and it could be wrongly understood by the witness whether she was actually -- while she was feeding these members or these civilians, whether she was made to wear a uniform or whether she was made to carry a gun. I would not relate it to the feeding as such, I would just ask her whether she was issued with a uniform and whether she was issued with a gun and leave it at that, and not specifically relating it to the distribution of food.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. But part of the point is whether her military service, if any, was related or carried out while distributing food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that you can ask then separately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I understand your point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, could you please answer the question of whether you were issued a uniform and whether you were issued a military weapon.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And so might I ask that, when you served food to the civilians, that you were neither dressed in a uniform nor were carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, during this time period, was your husband in any armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: He was mobilised, but he did not have a uniform. He wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And so would it be your testimony that both you and your husband were living as civilians in your brother-in-law and your sister-in-law's house in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally, we were civilians. We did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn your attention to September 17th of 1992, and would you please explain to the Trial Chamber whether the village of Novo Selo, where you were living, whether it was attacked or not.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did any people come into the house in which you were staying, specifically your brother-in-law's house, on that day when the village was attacked?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Two people came. Their names were Zenge. Zoran and I were there, and they killed my brother-in-law with a rifle barrel. They took me to a crossroads where they hit me under one eye, and my eye was injured. A neighbour of mine, Kadrija, whose last name I don't know, saved me from the knife. Muharem Sinanovic took me to a bar where my wounds were dressed, and then I was taken to the village of Bajrici. They took me to a room there. I was under a great deal of stress. They gave me a pill to calm down. They asked me about weapons and that sort of thing. I said I didn't know. I had come home from work in the evening, and when they arrested me, this man, Kadrija, whose last name I don't know, he said, "It's not her fault, she only came back last night." Whenever I meet Kadrija, I can tell him to his face, I'm not afraid of the truth, I'm not here to lie. I have three children and I do not want to lose my children. Over in Bajrici, there was a lot a lot of mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, I want to take you back to when you said that three people came into your house. First of all, can you explain to the Trial Chamber, who is Zoran?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: The one who was killed, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: He's the owner of the house. The host. I'm not sure how I should put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You mentioned that two men came into the room. Could you please describe what they were wearing, if anything.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Black, black clothes. All of them, they had socks or something over their heads, like a balaclava with an opening for the eyes and the mouth. They had black mittens on their hands. They didn't tell me anything, they just took me away. And then when Muharem Sinanovic took me to Bajrici, they told me that these people were --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, I'm sorry. I just wanted to go back to the men wearing black. Before you tell us who they were, would you please tell the Trial Chamber whether they carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you were struck under the eye. Were you struck under the eye with any article by these people?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: With a fist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a result of being struck under the eye, have you had any prolonged injuries or wounds?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a wound immediately, and there is a long-term injury to my eye. I can't see, and the doctor told me it was pointless to even try and treat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you describe the people as wearing the black clothing. Could you tell me, to your knowledge, did you know whether these people who were armed were Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Serbs or other people?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you come to find out who these people were?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: It was only later, when I was in Bajrici, they told me that they were ZNG. But I never asked anything about their ethnicity prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were there any other people, dressed similarly or dressed differently, who were around your house during the attack that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: The other people were wearing camouflage uniforms, and the two who took me away with black uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether any of the people wearing camouflage uniforms were Bosnian Serbs or Bosnian Muslims or another group?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: If they had been Bosnian Serbs, they wouldn't have fired at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then, would it be your testimony that they were not Bosnian Serbs, they might have been Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this person, Kadrija, who was actually very kind to you and saved you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then you were taken to have your wounds dressed. And did you ever see a person called Muharem Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Muharem took me there. Then there was a male nurse there called Refik. He is the brother of one of my colleagues who worked with me. He dressed my wounds three times and stopped the bleeding, and then Muharem Sinanovic took me to Bajrici. Along the way, he told me that he would let me go but that he was not allowed to let me go -- that he was prepared to let me go, but that he was not allowed to because otherwise they would kill him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that Muharem Sinanovic and Refik were very nice to you and treated you with respect?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is it also your testimony that, obviously, they were not able, it wasn't within their own free will, to release you or to let you go?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the village of Bajrici, could you tell the Trial Chamber what happened to you there?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: There were quite a lot of people there. Some spat at me and told me all sorts of things. Meanwhile, they took me to a room, brought me a tranquiliser of some kind. I was under a lot of stress. And then my first neighbour, Suljo Sulejmanovic - I think that's his last name - from Brdo came, and he asked me whether I knew who had hit me and why. I said it wasn't my fault, and I didn't know. And he said he would like to take me back to the confrontation line and hand me over to our forces. But that came to nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that he was unable to hand you over at the confrontation line because he was under the orders of another person?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, he was not allowed to do that. If I were in his place, I wouldn't have been allowed either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in Bajrici and you saw the other people, those that were cursing and spitting at you, could you tell the Trial Chamber whether they were Bosnian Muslims, Bosnian Serbs, or another group?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims, of course. For as long as I was in their village, it could not have been anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And did you see people dressed in uniforms or otherwise dressed in military apparatus or gear while you were in Bajrici?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: There were quite many of them in uniform. Those that were a bit older were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And once again, just for clarity's sake, were the people in uniform also Bosnian Muslims, or would you characterise them as Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, were you taken to a cellar of a house that day, after you arrived at Bajrici?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when they interrogated me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what type of questions did they ask you when they interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: They asked me whether the food was coming from, who the Chetniks were, where the weapons were coming from, and to confess. I said I didn't know, I only came last night. And during the interrogation, my neighbour, Suljo, came along and said, You can't ask any questions, she only came last night, and she's not to blame.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So was Suljo, a former neighbour of yours, another person you met with kindness as you were being held a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Another person, another person came, Mehmed Junuzovic, also from Bajrici. He was from nice, he and his wife Ajka. He brought me milk and sugar, and Ajka brought me pantaloons so that I could get a change of clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, is it true that even though there were people who were insulting you and yelling at you and people that were keeping you prisoner, that some persons, Bosnian Muslims, chose to treat you with kindness and respect under these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you then taken to a shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: The next morning, I was blindfolded and two people took me to the shelter, or cell, as they called it. They took my blindfold off, got me through a small door. They said that I should remain there, and that's where I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you just explain to the Trial Chamber the size or the dimensions of the shelter. How tall was it, how wide was it, how long was it, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: 4.50 by 4.50, and 1.50 in height.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, how many days or weeks did you stay at this shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: I remained at the shelter from the 18th of September, 1992 to the 4th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that I have -- we got this right. The transcript says "1.50 in height." In other words, in this shelter, could you stand up straight without touching the roof or the ceiling with your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you had to bend down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And am I correct in saying that you are 1 metre 57 centimetres tall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: During the time period that you stayed at the shelter, did you consider yourself to be a prisoner, someone unable to leave the shelter under their free will?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a prisoner. I couldn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when another person, a man named Nenad Lukic, did he come to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you please describe to the Trial Chamber the circumstances under which he came, and any conversations that the two of you had when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the time he came? The time, if that's what you mean, it was one afternoon; I really can't say because they took my watch away. He was tall, about 180, weighing about 78 or 80 kilos. He was blonde, he had civilian clothes, barefoot. His hands were tied up with a piece of wire in front of him, and he had a blindfold. He stayed there with me. He asked my name, I said Andja, and he said, You needn't be afraid. There is a policeman who has put in a word for you. His name is Omer. He said that he would have me exchanged, because he was able to do so, and that I would survive. Afterwards, he was taken away. I heard a moan somewhere above me. It was 2.00 at night. Sahbaz Muslimanovic had already arrived. He was a janitor. He asked me whether I needed to use the toilet --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: -- see me. I suppose that was something to look at. And I never heard of him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, could I kindly ask you to slow down, not to speak so fast, in other words, because we have interpreters in the various booths that are translating from your language to English and to French, and they are not catching up with you. Slow down a little bit, please, okay? Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, you stated that this person, Mr. Lukic, said that you would be -- you are protected, you would be exchanged. Did he tell you whether he also was protected and whether he would be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Some -- pardon me. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: He only said that they would kill him, that he would not be exchanged. And he said that I needn't be afraid because I would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, how long did he stay in the shelter with you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: An hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And how --

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Sixty minutes. Actually, 90. Sixty minutes is one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you remember how he was taken out of the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Two men came, able-bodied men. They took him out and beat him with a rifle butt, just outside the door. But that was all I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, could you, from inside the shelter, could you look outside the shelter and see what was happening in front?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So how were you able to see that he was beat with a rifle butt?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Just outside the door, they took him outside, the door was ajar. He had to bend down in order to get out, so that's how I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And were you able to clearly hear what you described as moaning from this Mr. Lukic, after he was taken outside?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber how the men who took Mr. Lukic outside were dressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, for sake of clarity, were they Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Serbs or another group?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, did there come a day when someone named Gumeni and Hosovka come to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: The second or third day they came.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And what happened, if anything, to you when they came to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, something happened. They opened the door. Needless to say, Gumeni made threats. He said I should reach out with my hands so he could take my rings off and my jewelry. He hit me with a piece of wood over the head. I had an injury which started bleeding. In the meantime, Hosovka came along and told him to stop beating me because she would be the one to interrogate me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So was Hosovka a woman?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you able to see how Gumeni and Hosovka were dressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were these black uniforms similar to the black uniforms that you described that the attackers wore on the 17th of September, as they entered your house?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you suffer physical injury from Gumeni and Hosovka that day?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Hosovka didn't even touch me, but Gumeni did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber exactly what it is that he did.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, he hit me on the head with a piece of wood and injured me here on the top of my head. Refik came over the next day and dressed my wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, once again, after an act of violence committed against you as a prisoner, then there was an act of kindness, of someone dressing your wounds the following day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would like to take you to another day when you were in the shelter. Did there come a time period where you heard voices or screaming from the outside, saying derogatory or slander against you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly what you mean. You mean when they came and -- there was an argument that could be heard with the policeman who was protecting me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And on that occasion, did someone threaten to cut your throat or to cut you to pieces?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Gumeni told me so, but then Mehmed Junuzovic came and the cop, and they said, Enough of this. Dzevad Demirovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then did this cop stop people from being able to come into the shelter and cause you physical harm?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: When he came, he chased them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when he acted and chased him away, did that mean on that occasion that you were not beaten up or in any way physically harmed or mentally harmed?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to that, yes. And then when Kojo came, no longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to stop at this time period, because then I'll be moving to another section. I think it would be appropriate to stop at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, I still want to ask you a couple more questions concerning your stay at the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I would ask at this time if we could go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Registrar, could we go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, did there come a time that you were taken out of the shelter and transferred to another place?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did you have hopes of being exchanged when you left the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Where did you think that you were going, then, when you left the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: To my death.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you left the shelter, were you accompanied by some of the people that you had met, such as Sadika?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Her husband was there. I met Vajka too, but I wasn't close with her. She would come to Bajrici with her husband, Mehmed Junuzovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, as you left the shelter, would you tell the Trial Chamber whether you were dressed traditionally, as someone who was a Bosnian Muslim or someone who was a Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: As a Bosnian Muslim, in pantaloons. And her name was Fata and not Andja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So was that the name that other people then called you, Fata, and not Andja?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Fata.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did you move with many of the Bosnian Muslims who were in the town to Cerska?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: With Sahbaz and another man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And is one of the reasons that you moved with the others is that there was shelling at some point in time of Kula Grad? I'm sorry, not at Kula Grad. The town you were in, from the direction of Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And would that be shelling, from your point of view, by Bosnian Serbs or by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: They told me that those were Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And isn't it true that the entire village was evacuated? And only because of that, you were released from the shelter.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: They told me that we all had to move further into some hills, and then we continued on to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Cerska, were you then taken to another place, a basement, and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber what the persons who interrogated you were wearing, if anything.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Automatic rifles and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, did you consider yourself still a prisoner, once you arrived at Cerska, after you had come with the evacuated village?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the men who interrogated you in Cerska, would you tell the Trial Chamber what type of information they asked for.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: They asked me how I came to be arrested, whether I'd been mobilised, who had brought me in, who interrogated me. Sahbaz brought in the papers, saying they had questioned her about everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And was it at that point, because Sahbaz brought in the papers, that the interrogation stopped?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, in that sense, Sahbaz assisted in halting the interrogation; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, after that time period, were you then taken to another place near Cerska that is referred to as the stable?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How did you come to be at the stable, meaning did you walk, did you ride? How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you accompanied by any other persons?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Only Sahbaz.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the stable, did you find other people in the stable?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you who those persons were, I'd like to ask you, did you still consider yourself then a prisoner, after being taken by Sahbaz to the stable?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he took me to the stable, so naturally I saw myself as a prisoner. I never believed that I would come out again, resurface.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you said that you saw other persons in the stable. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber who these other persons were that you saw when you arrived at the stable.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Rado Pejic, called Miso, from Gobelje, near Cerska; Branko Sekulic, from a place near Milici, born in 1967; Dragan Ilic, from Kasaba, arrested at Vlasenica bridge, born in 1975; and Jakov Dzokic, who was returning home from his mandatory JNA military service, arrested on the road. These four people were there when I arrived in the stable.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, had you known any of those persons before?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you describe to the Trial Chamber, upon your arrival, what was the physical appearance of Branko Sekulic?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Branko Sekulic looked normal. He had a wound to his left heel, but he was able to walk. He could see, he could hear. However, after being severely beaten by Alaga, he became deaf.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Could you now tell the Trial Chamber, what was the physical appearance of Jakov Dzokic?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: He looked tall, skinny. None of them had bruises when I arrived. Later on, they would be beaten every day. I would be beaten too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And also, with Dragan Ilic, did he also look as you've just described, at that point, not beaten?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at the point when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And then lastly, Mr. Rado Pejic, could you please describe what he looked like when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: He was shorter than the other three. He was rather pale in his face. He was on the quiet side. He did not have any bruises. None of them had any bruises when I arrived. Later on, we would be beaten regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the name Alaga. Who was Alaga?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: A Muslim, young man. I don't know his actual name, I just heard him being referred to as Alaga.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, is he one of the persons, or a person who participated in beating the men who were in the stable?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: He was a school friend of Branko Sekulic, and Branko said, Remember when they gave us bad grades? That's when the beating started. It was quite difficult for me when I saw Branko bleed from his nose and on his face. And then he told me to stand up and stay about 1 metre from the wall. He hit me and I fainted, and when I came to, one of the four of them told me that he kicked me in the chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: For clarity, when you said that he told you to stand up against the wall, are you referring to Alaga or Branko?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Alaga. Alaga.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So were you ever physically mistreated by Alaga?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: He slapped me and beat me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when he beat you to the point of unconsciousness?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: I've just told you, he kicked me in the chest and I fainted. When I regained consciousness, I saw that I was wet. They poured water on me. My fellow prisoners told me that he had kicked me in the chest. I don't remember that myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, was Alaga wearing any form of uniform, or was he dressed as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: He was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified to the Trial Chamber that the men who were in the stable received various beatings. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber who were the types of persons who administered these beatings to Branko, Jakov, Dragan, and Rado?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you their names. I don't know their names. I just know that Branko told us that one man's name was Alaga, and that they had been at school together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether the men who administered the beatings were wearing uniforms or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And can we just confirm that the men were Bosnian Muslims, or were they Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, how long did you and the four men stay at the stable, in terms of days or weeks or months?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed at the stable from the 5th of October, 1992, until the 26th of January, 1993. I don't know when they got there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And during that time period at the stable, were you able to see the physical mistreatment of the four men, and any bruises or wounds that were caused by the beatings or physical mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a lot of physical mistreatment, beating. I saw that personally at the stable. The men were beaten there. I would get my fair portion as well. They didn't kick me like they kicked the men, but they slapped me on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And because of the beatings that you received and the men received, did that, in some manner, assist the five of you in bonding together?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: I think it did. While we were there together at the stable, they didn't take us any place else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you whether there were guards posted near the stable during the time period that you and the four men were present.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the stable. They had a little hut made out of wood and covered with tarpaulin. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How many guards were posted outside of the stable?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Two. They rotated, worked in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, would it be your testimony that, at all times, you and the other men were guarded and unable to escape from the stable?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, was one of the people who guarded the stable also the turnkey, the person who had the keys to the stable?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know who had the keys to the stable to allow you or the others in or out?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: I was told that Adem Huric had the key. I saw him when they took us out, and I couldn't really tell you now. I don't know who they got the key from.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, would you just describe for the Trial Chamber the physical layout or dimensions of the stable.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: The stable was 6 metres long, 4 metres wide, 2 metres high. It was made out of concrete blocks. It was covered with roof tiles. The floor was just a plain dirt floor, covered with straw. The door was a wooden door. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And at times, were you and your fellow prisoners taken outside to get a bit of fresh air?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Were you ever allowed to contact your family while you were at the stable?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Registrar, could we go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Radovic, did there come a time period when you and the other four prisoners left the stable in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 26th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber how you came to leave the stable?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening, the guards told us that we would be exchanged the following day, that we would go to Srebrenica and be exchanged there. In the morning, they brought us breakfast, beans. Zulfo Tursunovic came, and another person called Nindza. They acted quite decently, I can't say anything else. They didn't even touch us, any of us prisoners. On our way there, we had to descend from the hill, because the stable is at the hill, and then when we reached the bottom, a soldier joined us. He hit Branko once. And we went on foot towards Srebrenica. Branko was wounded and could not continue. He stayed at a stable, and we travelled the whole day, up until 8 in the evening, to get to Srebrenica. We passed through Kravica --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Ms. Radovic, I'd ask you again to slow down a little bit, and I want to go back and ask you some questions about the leaving. Okay. You've described, or you've talked about, a man named Zulfo Tursunovic. Could you please describe what he looked like to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Zulfo looked like a decent person, quite tall, large, wore a camouflage uniform, had automatic rifle, pistol, and a Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zulfo was based in Cerska or whether he came from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think he was from Cerska, because he never visited us there. He probably got there on somebody else's instructions, to take us to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, the other people who were with Zulfo, could you just tell the Trial Chamber what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Also, in uniforms, I remember that Nindza had blue eyes. They were also armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did it appear that, among the three of them, Zulfo and the two other people that you've just described to us, did it appear as if Zulfo was a person who had some type of authority or command over the other two?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, because they asked him for everything, and his words were complied with by the other two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, did Zulfo have any form of communication with him, a radio or some method in which he could communicate with others, other than just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think she has already told us that he was carrying a Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sorry, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: During the time period that you were with Zulfo, did he ever use the Motorola?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: He lagged behind for a while. He walked behind us, most likely because he communicated with someone. But we didn't dare turn back, turn around, to look at that. We continued on to Srebrenica, and we got to a creek and stopped there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, on your way to Srebrenica, do you know what towns that you passed through?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: I just know that they told us that we had passed through Kravica. I don't know those places, because I'd never been there before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you and the four men who were in prison with you left the stable together. Did all of you arrive in Srebrenica together?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No. Branko was unable; he stayed behind in the stable, or a shed. He arrived on horseback the next morning. But the four of us did go, and we arrived, the three of them and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Did one of the armed guards stay behind with Branko?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, you said that you had walked all throughout the day. By the time you arrived in Srebrenica, was it evening, was it nighttime, or was it still late afternoon?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: Nighttime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Srebrenica, were you asked to give your names to anyone?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't ask our names. They had a list with our names, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I wanted to show one exhibit. I don't know whether we have enough time, or whether we should continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've got two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would prefer if we would not use these two minutes with the exhibit, in case the witness would want to take a bit more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I would suggest too. So, Madam Radovic, we have to stop here for today, and we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00, I think, in this same courtroom, if I remember well. I thank you, and see you all tomorrow. Madam, one very important thing is that, between today and tomorrow, please do not communicate with anyone or talk to anyone in connection with the matters that you are testifying upon. That's very important. And don't let anyone, also, contact you or talk to you about these things, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
